title: Solar energy development and aquatic ecosystems in the Southwestern United States: Potential Impacts, Mitigation, and Research Needs
abstract: The cumulative impacts of utility-scale solar energy facilities on aquatic ecosystems in the Southwestern United States are of concern, considering the many existing regional anthropogenic stressors. We review the potential impacts of solar energy development on aquatic habitat and biota. The greatest potential for impacts is related to the loss, fragmentation, or prolonged drying of ephemeral water bodies and drainage networks resulting from the loss of desert washes within the construction footprint of the facility. Groundwater-dependent aquatic habitat may also be affected by operational groundwater withdrawal in the case of water-intensive solar technologies. Solar panels have also been found to attract aquatic insects and waterbirds, potentially resulting in mortality. Avoiding construction activity near perennial and intermittent surface waters is the primary means of reducing impacts on aquatic habitats, followed by measures to minimize erosion, sedimentation, and contaminant inputs into waterways. Currently, significant data gaps make solar facility impact assessment and mitigation more difficult. Examples include the need for more regional and site-specific studies of surface–groundwater connectivity, more detailed maps of regional stream networks and riparian vegetation corridors, as well as surveys of the aquatic communities inhabiting ephemeral streams. In addition, because they often lack regulatory protection, there is also a need to develop valuation criteria for ephemeral waters based on their ecological and hydrologic function within the landscape. By addressing these research needs, we can achieve the goal of greater reliance on solar energy, while at the same time minimizing impacts on desert ecosystems.

# Solar Energy Development and Aquatic Ecosystems in the Southwestern United States: Potential Impacts, Mitigation, and Research Needs

Mark Grippo[•] John W. Hayse[•] Ben L. O’Connor

Received: 8 April 2014 / Accepted: 9 October 2014 / Published online: 21 October 2014  Springer Science+Business Media New York 2014

Abstract The cumulative impacts of utility-scale solar energy facilities on aquatic ecosystems in the Southwestern United States are of concern, considering the many existing regional anthropogenic stressors. We review the potential impacts of solar energy development on aquatic habitat and biota. The greatest potential for impacts is related to the loss, fragmentation, or prolonged drying of ephemeral water bodies and drainage networks resulting from the loss of desert washes within the construction footprint of the facility. Groundwater-dependent aquatic habitat may also be affected by operational groundwater withdrawal in the case of water-intensive solar technologies. Solar panels have also been found to attract aquatic insects and waterbirds, potentially resulting in mortality. Avoiding construction activity near perennial and intermittent surface waters is the primary means of reducing impacts on aquatic habitats, followed by measures to minimize erosion, sedimentation, and contaminant inputs into waterways. Currently, significant data gaps make solar facility impact assessment and mitigation more difficult. Examples include the need for more regional and site-specific studies of surface–groundwater connectivity, more detailed maps of regional stream networks and riparian vegetation corridors,

as well as surveys of the aquatic communities inhabiting ephemeral streams. In addition, because they often lack regulatory protection, there is also a need to develop valuation criteria for ephemeral waters based on their ecological and hydrologic function within the landscape. By addressing these research needs, we can achieve the goal of greater reliance on solar energy, while at the same time minimizing impacts on desert ecosystems.

Keywords Solar energy  Aquatic ecology  Renewable energy  Environmental impacts  Water use  Watershed management

## Introduction

With recent improvements in technology, solar energy is rapidly approaching economic competitiveness with fossil fuels (Fthenakis et al. 2009). Much of the electricity currently generated by solar energy is derived from smallscale, distributed sources in the form of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) cells placed on houses and office buildings. However, there is also great interest in developing utilityscale solar energy facilities (hereafter referred to as solar facilities) in the Southwestern United States because of the high regional solar irradiance, and, consequently, high electricity generation potential (Fig. 1). Further solar facility development will be spurred by renewable portfolio standards (RPSs), which have been adopted by several Southwestern states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, and Utah), with some requiring up to 33 % of that state’s electricity to be generated from renewables by 2020 (Table 1). Several solar facilities are currently operational on private lands, and additional facilities are planned or under construction that would

In addition, the U.S. Department of the Interior Bureau of Land Management (BLM), which administers millions of acres of public land in the Southwestern United States, has designated solar energy zones (SEZs) on public lands in California, Colorado, Arizona, Utah, New Mexico, and Nevada, where the BLM proposes to prioritize commercial solar energy development (BLM and DOE 2012) (Fig. 2). Currently, there are more than 40 pending or approved permit applications for solar developments on public lands that are under review by the BLM (http://blmsolar.anl.gov/documents/docs/Pending_applications_ list.pdf).

Commercial solar power technology can be categorized as (1) concentrating solar power (CSP) technologies, which create electrical power using the sun’s energy to produce heat or steam to drive a generator, and (2) PV technologies, which use solar cells to create

power by directly converting photons into electricity (Singh 2013; Zhang et al. 2013). Examples of PV technologies include both the simple, relatively inexpensive, flat-plate PV, and the more efficient concentrating PV technology that tracks the sun and reflects the sunlight onto solar cells (Singh 2013). Examples of CSP technologies include parabolic trough, compact linear fresnel reflector (CLFR), and solar power tower (Zhang et al. 2013). For CSP technology, the produced steam can be cooled with water (wet cooling) or air (dry cooling). Although power towers have potentially greater efficiency than parabolic troughs, trough technology is well developed and has been in use for decades.

Currently, there are multiple existing anthropogenic stressors on aquatic ecosystems in arid regions, including dams, surface and groundwater withdrawal, urbanization, mining, the introduction of invasive species, and homogenization of aquatic habitat (Mueller and Marsh 2002;

Fig. 2 Bureau of Land Management designated solar energy zones located on public lands in the Southwestern United States (Source BLM and DOE 2012)

Fitzhugh and Richter 2004). In addition to these stressors, climate change is also a significant source of ecosystem change, with most climate models for the Southwestern United States indicating future increases in temperature, evapotranspiration, extreme weather events, and decreasing rainfall and snowmelt in some areas (Seager et al. 2007; Archer and Predick 2008). If not properly implemented, the large-scale construction of solar facilities in desert environments could significantly add to these existing stressors.

As in humid climates, a primary function of water bodies in desert regions is to provide physical and biological connectivity across the landscape. Intermittent and ephemeral streams transport water originating from upland snowmelt and precipitation to downstream perennial reaches, thereby maintaining flow and recharging groundwater (Izbicki 2002; Larned et al. 2010; Smith et al. 2011). In addition to hydrologic connectivity, the downstream transport of sediment, nutrients, minerals, and organic matter is a critical function of intermittent and ephemeral streams (Larned et al. 2010).

Existing studies also strongly suggest a critical role for intermittent and ephemeral waters in supporting both endemic and migratory aquatic and terrestrial biota (Levick et al. 2008; Steward et al. 2012). Although intermittent and ephemeral waters generally do not support permanent aquatic communities, they are important seasonal habitat for biota with aquatic life stages such as amphibians, branchiopod crustaceans, and a wide variety of aquatic insect species (Brode and Bury 1984; Graham 2002; Sponseller et al. 2010). Riparian corridors along ephemeral channels are used as reproductive habitat by terrestrial species like birds (Austin 1970), mammals (Stamp and

Ohmart 1979), and reptiles (Brode and Bury 1984). Riparian vegetation forms long stretches of contiguous habitat that wildlife can use to travel across the landscape (Knopf et al. 1988). These riparian corridors provide food, relief from thermal stress, and predator avoidance for both terrestrial and aquatic biota (Krueper 1993; Jennings 1997; Levick et al. 2008). Dry streams are also favorable for long-distance movements because of the lack of anthropogenic obstructions and the presence of organic matter, moist sediments, and periodic isolated pools (Steward et al. 2012). Intermittent and ephemeral waters also support several federally listed plant and animal species, some of which are endemic to specific springs, wetlands, or streams, and, consequently, are highly vulnerable to extinction if their habitat is degraded by human activities. These species include both aquatic biota and terrestrial biota that are found in association with surface water features. Johnson (1989) estimated that riparian habitats are required by 70 % of threatened and endangered vertebrate species in Arizona during some period in their life history. Thus, in contrast to the common perception of deserts as lifeless, intermittent and ephemeral water bodies can support relatively diverse aquatic and terrestrial biotic communities, which greatly enhance local, watershed, and regional biodiversity (Haukos and Smith 2003; Levick et al. 2008).

Despite the importance of intermittent and ephemeral streams and the number of proposed solar facilities, no peer-reviewed assessments have specifically focused on the potential ecological impacts of solar development on aquatic habitat and biota (see Lovich and Ennen 2011 for a review of potential solar energy impacts on terrestrial

wildlife). The primary objective of this paper is to review the potential impacts of utility-scale solar energy development on aquatic habitat and associated biological communities, with particular emphasis on intermittent (seasonally dry stream, especially during times of low rainfall or high heat) and ephemeral waters (defined as those that do not receive groundwater inputs and contain water only briefly and in direct response to precipitation), which are estimated to compose more than 80 % of streams in the Desert Southwest (Levick et al. 2008). We will first describe the potential impacts on aquatic systems from solar energy development, as well as minimization and mitigation measures to reduce ecological impacts on aquatic habitat. Then we will discuss significant knowledge gaps and research needs concerning the impacts of solar facilities on hydrology and aquatic ecosystem function. This paper complements existing reviews discussing the

## Potential Impacts from Utility-Scale Solar Facilities

## Construction Phase

One of the main impacts from a solar energy project, regardless of the technology utilized, is the amount of aquatic habitat lost or modified within the construction footprint. For example, the total statewide SEZ area designated by the BLM ranges from 24.5 to 621.7 km[2] (Table 2), although not all of the area within the SEZs is likely to be used for solar development. The size of individual solar facilities will vary based on the planned power generation capacity and technology employed (Table 3). Estimates given in the solar Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement (PEIS) for a range of technologies (BLM and DOE 2012), indicate that solar facility footprints vary between 0.02 and 0.04 km[2] /MW (Table 3). For example, a 400-MW power tower or PV facility would occupy about 14 km[2] , whereas a 400-MW parabolic trough facility would require about 8 km[2] .

could be affected by construction activities. For example, on public lands, the estimated intermittent and ephemeral stream length within SEZs ranges as high as 1,052 km for California (Table 2). In addition, the stream lengths may be underestimated because the National Hydrography Dataset on which these lengths are based may significantly underestimate the actual number of streams (Caruso 2011). Although the entire SEZ will not be cleared and graded, there is still a significant length of stream that will be affected by solar energy development.

Direct disturbance to intermittent and ephemeral waters would result from site grading and from modifying flow pathways to avoid the erosion of facility infrastructure. Consequently, significant changes in surface water flow could affect the transport of sediment, nutrients, minerals, and organic matter that maintains habitat and geomorphological processes in downstream reaches (Webb et al. 2000; Izbicki 2002, 2007; Larned et al. 2010; Smith et al. 2011). Although species in arid environments are generally adapted to temporary drying, the abundance and composition of animal communities would be altered in streams experiencing significant changes in the timing, duration, velocity, and magnitude of surface flow (Stanley et al. 1994; Lake 2003; Sada et al. 2005; Archer and Predick 2008; McCluney and Sabo 2011; Datry 2012). Similarly, construction-related hydrologic changes could also affect vegetation communities, as the distribution, density, diversity, and species composition of vascular plant communities are largely determined by flow (Stromberg et al. 2009; Katz et al. 2011). For example, Schlesinger et al. (1989) found lower biomass of desert shrub species in areas experiencing flow diversions compared with areas receiving natural surface flow.

In addition to the loss of aquatic habitat and hydrologic modification, the construction of large-scale solar facilities could degrade water quality by a number of mechanisms. Contaminants could be introduced as a result of the accidental release of fuels, lubricants, or pesticides/herbicides and dust suppressant chemicals used during the construction period (Lovich and Ennen 2011). Construction activities would also increase sedimentation in localized areas by removing riparian vegetation and disturbing desert pavement and biological crusts (soil surface communities composed primarily of cyanobacteria, mosses, and lichens), which contribute to soil stability (Bowker et al. 2008; Wood et al. 2005; Belnap et al. 2012). Once disturbed, desert pavement and biological crusts can take many years to recover (Belnap and Eldridge 2003; Viles 2008). Thus, ground-disturbing activities in general could result in long-term changes in water and windborne soil deposition into aquatic habitat, potentially increasing turbidity and the concentrations of dissolved solids, salts, and metals (Field et al. 2010).

As with earlier human development in the Southwest, access roads, pipelines, and transmission lines could extend for great distances from the solar facility to more urban areas where the power is in greatest demand (Lovich and Bainbridge 1999). Consequently, there is a high probability that these structures will intersect surface waters, given the remote location of many solar facilities. The impacts of stream crossings on aquatic habitat have been described in several reviews (Lovich and Bainbridge 1999; Trombulak and Frissell 2000; Spellerberg 1998; Castro et al. 2014). These impacts include flow alteration, sedimentation, displacement of aquatic biota, and contaminant runoff. Several mitigation measures can be used to reduce impacts at individual stream crossings, but cumulative impacts could be significant.

## Operations

The application of dust suppressants will occur throughout the operational period, where they could enter aquatic habitats following rainfall. Dust suppressants are used to reduce the deposition of dust on mirrors and panels (Lovich and Ennen 2011) and consist primarily of chloride salts and brines. They can come in a number of other chemical forms, however, including natural carbohydrates and fibers, clay, hydrocarbons, and synthetic polymers (Gillies et al. 1999). Dust suppressants have been found to increase runoff into streams (Singh et al. 2003), potentially resulting in scour impacts on aquatic communities. The toxicity of some dust suppressants is not well studied, even though they are considered to pose a potential threat to aquatic habitats (Steevens et al. 2007). For example, salts are known to enter waterways where they can increase water column stratification, reduce dissolved oxygen, promote the growth of nuisance algae (Ramakrishna and Viraraghavan 2005), and increase salinity to levels that are toxic to riparian vegetation, fish, amphibians, and aquatic invertebrates (Karraker et al. 2008). Other dust suppressants, including lignin, sulfonate, and petroleum-based chemicals, also pose a risk to aquatic biota. For example, an accidental release of the dust suppressant Coherex[] into a stream resulted in high mortality of fish and aquatic invertebrates, although the impacts were short term and sediments recovered quickly (Ettinger 1987). However, runoff from soils treated with multiple dust suppressants (surfactants, synthetic organics, and synthetic polymers) was not found to be toxic to fish, algae, or aquatic invertebrates for most treatments (Irwin 2008).

would require water for washing mirrors or panels and for potable water, there are significant differences in total water demands among the technologies. Most parabolic trough and power tower facilities require steam for driving turbines, necessitating far higher water demands than PV (Table 3). Dry cooling and hybrid cooling systems use significantly less water than wet cooling systems (Burkhardt et al. 2011), which can require more water than conventional power generation from coal (Sovacool and Sovacool 2009). Thus, steam-generating facilities that use wet cooling have the greatest potential for water depletion impacts on aquatic habitats.

The BLM estimated groundwater drawdown at the SEZs over a 20-year facility operational period under different technology scenarios. Drawdown was typically less than 1 m for all low water use PV technology and up to 15 m for CSP with dry cooling scenarios (Table 4). For the high

pumping (CSP with wet cooling) scenarios, groundwater drawdown was as high as 110 m for the largest SEZ. Although many solar facilities will utilize PV technology, most solar facility permit applications submitted to the BLM are for the more water-intensive dry-cooled CSP technology (Table 3; http://blmsolar.anl.gov/documents/docs/Pending_ applications_list.pdf). Any additional water use could be problematic for the basins that are already overpumped, and the accuracy of the drawdown estimates is uncertain because both the sustainable yield of groundwater basins and the actual pumping needs of solar energy projects are not well characterized. In addition, although construction-related water withdrawal would occur only within a relatively short time frame, the amount of water used would be significant and potentially greater than the total water use during the operational period (Klise et al. 2013). Groundwater levels in the Southwestern United States have declined significantly over the last few decades (Zektser et al. 2005), and groundwater outputs currently exceed recharge rates at many of the potential BLM-designated SEZs (BLM and DOE 2012). Excessive groundwater withdrawal could result in depletion impacts on pools or spring-fed streams that rely on the groundwater source for recharge. In intermittent and perennial habitats, water withdrawal could reduce water depth and the frequency and duration of wet periods, which could ultimately increase the habitat fragmentation of stream networks by converting flowing water into pools separated by dry reaches. In addition to spatial and temporal reduction in available aquatic habitat, the water quality of the remaining habitat could decrease as temperature and solute concentrations increase and dissolved oxygen levels decrease (Zektser et al. 2005).

A number of impacts on plant and animal communities resulting from excessive groundwater use have also been documented. In the Southwestern United States, the decline in groundwater elevation due to groundwater withdrawal has been shown to reduce riparian tree density and shift species composition to more xeric plants (Zektser et al. 2005; Webb and Leake 2006). In addition, increased salinity from reduced flow can facilitate the establishment of invasive species such as Tamarix ramosissima (Cleverly et al. 1997; Smith et al. 1998). Water withdrawal concerns are particularly relevant in aquifers supporting endangered species. For example, habitat for the Devils Hole pupfish (Cyprinodon nevadensis mionectes) underwent significant depth declines beginning in the 1960s because of water withdrawals for irrigation (Riggs and Deacon 2004).

Visual attractants, such as polarized light and the presence of permanent evaporation ponds, are another longterm operational concern associated with solar facilities. Water polarizes sunlight, which serves as a visual cue that attracts waterbirds and aquatic insects. Solar panels polarize light more strongly than water (Horva ́th et al.

2009), and, consequently, aquatic insects appear to be more attracted to solar panels than actual water bodies (Horva ́th et al. 2010). In this way, solar energy facilities may act as large-scale ‘‘ecological traps’’ where aquatic insects lay eggs on solar panels (Horva ́th et al. 2009), resulting in mortality and wasted reproductive effort.

Because of the number of bird deaths recently reported at several utility-scale solar energy facilities, avian mortality has emerged as a primary concern among stakeholders and environmental managers. There are few peerreviewed studies of bird deaths at solar facilities. In one study of a 10-MW solar power tower, McCrary et al. (1986) recorded 57 bird deaths over a 40-week period primarily from collision with heliostats, and an additional 13 deaths from the heat generated by the heliostats. While the authors were not able to definitively cite casual factors, many of the deaths recorded were aquatic species like teals, grebes, coots, and sandpipers that could have mistaken the panels for water or been attracted to evaporation ponds located on the site.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service conducted a preliminary analysis of incidental bird deaths reported from a PV facility, a parabolic trough facility, and a power tower facility (Kagan et al. 2014). Although the cause of death could not be determined for many of the birds, collision, and predation (potentially following collision) appeared to be the leading cause of death at the PV and trough facilities. Bird mortality at the power tower site was primarily the result of burning and to a lesser degree, collision (Kagan et al. 2014). Although a wide variety of dead bird

species were recorded, a greater proportion of waterbirds were found at the PV facility, while aerial and terrestrial species were proportionally higher at the trough and power tower sites. This suggests that aquatic-oriented birds may be disproportionately affected by PV technology or the presence of ponds at the site (Kagan et al. 2014).

While solar panels can cumulatively kill large numbers of bird and aquatic insects, it is not known whether the mortality is great enough to produce a population-level effect. The mortality data analyzed in Kagan et al. (2014) were not collected using a systematic survey design, thus the actual number of deaths over a specific time period could not be determined. McCrary et al. (1986) estimated the mortality rate associated with the solar facility represented a negligible portion of the local bird populations. However, the power tower he examined was only 10 MW, and the newer facilities are generally greater than 200 MW (http://blmso lar.anl.gov/documents/docs/Pending_applications_list.pdf).

A potential increase in fire risk resulting from the loss of coolant or the combustion of stored oil has also been associated with utility-scale solar energy development (Mills 2004; Tsoutsosa et al. 2005). Fire would impact aquatic habitat by destroying riparian vegetation, which would be slow to recover in deserts systems (Brooks and Matchett 2006). However, the chances of a wildfire would be significantly reduced by vegetation clearing (including fire-conducive invasive vegetation) on the grounds of the facility (Brooks and Matchett 2006) and the implementation of a fire safety and response plan that included fuel inventories and breaks.

## Mitigation Measures to Protect Aquatic Resources

A mitigation hierarchy is a systematic approach to land development that emphasizes avoidance as the primary mitigation priority followed by minimization measures for those impacts that are unavoidable. Following a mitigation hierarchy approach allows the development of renewable energy, while at the same time minimizing environmental impacts or resource use conflicts, and facilitates the environmental permitting process for solar energy developers (Cameron et al. 2012). Avoiding surface water, wetland, and riparian areas is the primary way to reduce ecological impacts on aquatic systems (Table 5). For unavoidable impacts, the following minimization measures would reduce the magnitude of impacts on surface waters:

- Mapping of local surface water networks and quantifying the sustainable groundwater yield, considering both the solar facility withdrawals and existing water rights and management plans.

- Use of numerical groundwater and surface hydrology models to assess the potential for surface flow disturbance and groundwater withdrawals to affect habitats that support special status species (see research and monitoring needs).

- Minimization or elimination of groundwater-related impacts by using low water use technology like PV. In addition, water could be trucked into meet water needs during the construction and operational periods.

Impacts on aquatic habitat from erosion and runoff would be minimized by:

- Implementation of effective stormwater management plans and following best management practices regarding stream buffers.

- Development of a rapid assessment tool to quantitatively evaluate the vulnerability of streams to erosion and identify stream reaches where the allocation of mitigation and monitoring resources are most needed (Bledsoe et al. 2012).

- Minimization of changes in runoff patterns by mapping and subsequently avoiding biological crusts and desert pavement (Viles 2008; Bowker et al. 2008; Wood et al. 2005). In addition to field surveys, biological crusts and desert pavement can be mapped using remote sensing (Hibbitts and Gillespie 2008; Nagendra et al. 2013).

## Research and Monitoring Needs

In the coming years, the results of mitigation and compliance monitoring plans required for solar facility projects on BLM-administered lands will provide a much better

understanding of the physical impacts of solar energy development on intermittent and ephemeral waters. However, additional monitoring studies will be needed to investigate the ecological impacts on plant and animal communities and to assess the effectiveness of mitigation measures. Recent reviews have stressed the lack of available monitoring data and consequent uncertainty about the ecological impacts of solar energy development (Turney and Fthenakis 2011; Lovich and Ennen 2011; Northrup and Wittemyer 2013; Hernandez et al. 2014). This uncertainty may lead to unnecessary delays in project permitting, or, conversely, allow projects to proceed where future impacts are significant but unknown.

Considering the current state of management uncertainty, an adaptive management approach is particularly useful because it relies on iterative hypothesis testing to determine how well management policies achieve the desired management goals (McLain and Lee 1996). In the context of solar energy development, the management policies would generally be construction and operational requirements designed to minimize impacts. Monitoring plays a critical role in adaptive management by providing data to confirm that the policy is meeting its objective, or whether it needs to be refined, implemented, or retested (Lyons et al. 2008; Lindenmayer and Likens 2009). Effective mitigation measures required for current projects would then be implemented in monitoring and mitigation plans for future solar energy facilities.

As described below, in developing adaptive monitoring and mitigation plans, several areas of study would address existing data gaps concerning both the impacts of solar energy development on aquatic resources and the effectiveness of proposed mitigation plans. For these studies, it is critical to collect baseline (pre-construction) data; in many cases, it will be necessary to use a before-aftercontrol impact (BACI) design (Underwood 1994; Lovich and Ennen 2011) or transect sampling designs that can detect spatial changes in plant and animal communities at different distances from the solar facility.

## Groundwater Withdrawal Impacts

Effectively monitoring long-term impacts from solar energy facilities requires establishing a baseline groundwater status and the mapping of groundwater-dependent biological communities, both regionally, and in specific areas proposed for solar energy development. Regional groundwater models have been developed for the Mojave Desert and the Great Basin (Patten et al. 2008). Linking these regional models to local groundwater models is necessary to accurately predict local changes in groundwater conditions resulting from water withdrawal for solar facility operations. In addition to model development, basic

data on surface–groundwater interactions at the local scale are often inadequate for informing the groundwater models (Patten et al. 2008). More intensive data collection (e.g., additional gaging stations and monitoring wells) and more research on hydrologic connectivity between groundwater basins would improve our understanding of the offsite impacts of groundwater withdrawal for solar facility operations.

In addition to direct groundwater monitoring, bioindicators can be used to assess the current status and future changes in surface–groundwater connections. The loss of groundwater-dependent phreatophytic plants species is frequently observed following groundwater depletions (Patten et al. 2008), as is the loss of halophytic plants if a decline in groundwater discharge decreases the salt concentration at the soil surface (Patten et al. 2008). Therefore, mapping groundwater-dependent systems could be used to identify and monitor aquatic systems within the basin that are most vulnerable to solar facility–related groundwater withdrawals. For example, Howard and Merrifield (2010) developed a hydrologic unit code (HUC) 12 level index of ecosystem groundwater dependency for California using geographic information system (GIS) data on the location of wetland vegetation, along with hydrologic indicators like stream baseflow and the location of springs and seeps. Remote sensing is also an effective method for mapping groundwater-dependent communities. Two moderate resolution imaging spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite imagery products, the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and normalized difference wetness index (NDWI) are commonly used to measure aboveground plant biomass and productivity and vegetation moisture content and evapotranspiration, respectively (Shupe and Marsh 2004; van Leeuwen et al. 2010; Casady et al. 2013). Barron et al. (2012) monitored photosynthetic biomass and evapotranspiration over the year using NDVI and NDWI, and they identified areas of groundwater-dependent vegetation by their persistent growth and relatively high leaf moisture even during seasonal dry periods.

## Disturbances to Surface Hydrology

Small, ephemeral washes are prevalent throughout the desert landscape to such a degree that direct impacts on these features are to some extent unavoidable. Site grading and construction activities that modify or eliminate these ephemeral channels will change streamflow patterns, hydrologic regime, and instream physical and chemical conditions, both onsite and in downstream areas. Consequently, there is a need to devise engineering strategies that meet the developer’s need to protect facility infrastructure from flooding while at the same time minimizing the alteration in offsite flow regime. Research should focus on

hypothesis testing of engineering plans for channel rerouting that best maintain the natural hydrology in downstream surface waters and riparian habitats. For new streams created to meet mitigation requirements, there is also a need to develop channel engineering designs with regard to channel slope, drop structures, and bank morphology that achieves the desired hydrologic (i.e., sediment transport) and biological (vegetation communities species composition and cover) functions of streams.

Vegetation communities are excellent monitoring endpoints for assessing surface hydrologic disturbance because of the species-specific sensitivity to soil moisture, flood intensity, and flow frequency and duration (Stromberg et al. 2005, 2010). Under decreasing flow, plant composition can shift to more xeric species, and riparian herbaceous cover may be reduced (Smith et al. 1998; Stromberg et al. 2005, 2010). Vegetation mapping and condition indices developed for regions in which solar facilities are proposed could serve as a baseline that can be used to assess impacts from solar facilities. For example, using remote sensing, changes in vegetation composition (including invasive species), density, cover, and phenology can be monitored over time (Nagendra et al. 2013) following solar facility construction. Although remote sensing holds great promise as a monitoring tool in desert systems (van Leeuwen et al. 2010; Casady et al. 2013), more work is needed to develop algorithms to accurately map vegetation community structure and phenology at the regional and site-specific level.

## Avian and Insect Attraction to Solar Energy Facilities

It has been demonstrated that solar facility infrastructure can result in the direct mortality and reproductive failure of large numbers of aquatic insects and waterbirds (Horva ́th et al. 2010; Kagan et al. 2014). Although the populationlevel effects of polarized lights on insects and their predators could be minor, this has not been verified experimentally. Well-designed monitoring studies are the primary research needed to understand the causes and magnitude of avian and insect mortality. Continuous monitoring of infrastructure using infrared video and radar technology could be used to quantify the number of bird interactions with the solar facility. Bird mortality surveys employing a BACI design would be most effective in estimating project-specific mortality in relation to natural mortality. Regional and site-specific preconstruction estimates of the number of resident and migratory bird numbers are also needed to assess the significance of bird mortality to waterbird populations.

Measures to reduce the attractiveness of solar facilities to waterbirds and aquatic insects are another research need.

Maintaining vegetation-free areas around solar infrastructure, reducing bird access to ponds, and minimizing vertical mirror orientation, have all been suggested as ways to reduce waterbird mortality (McCrary et al. 1986; Kagan et al. 2014). However, the effectiveness of these mitigation measures has not been verified experimentally. Modifications to the panels themselves are another potential mitigation measure. For example, recent studies have demonstrated that white borders are effective in reducing the attractiveness of solar panels to aquatic insects (Horva ́th et al. 2010), which suggests that modifying solar panels in this manner could be an effective mitigation tool. However, such modifications face trade-offs with other considerations, including the potential increase in visual impacts and a reduction in the energy generation capacity of the panel.

## Development of Functional Valuation Criteria for Ephemeral Waters

At the federal level, Section 404 of the clean water act (CWA) regulates the discharge of dredged or fill material into waters of the United States. CWA compliance and costly compensatory mitigation requirements would likely limit solar facility construction on or near major perennial and intermittent channels. However, protections for ephemeral waters are less clear. Ephemeral washes are dominant landscape features, and avoiding all washes within a development site would not typically be possible. Recent Supreme Court decisions significantly reduced the CWA’s traditionally expansive wetland protections (Caruso 2011). This suggests that ephemeral water features need to have a ‘‘significant nexus’’ to perennial waters by contributing to their physical, chemical, and biological integrity (Caruso and Haynes 2011). The significant nexus to perennial water features is problematic for intermittent and ephemeral waters which may not have a surface connection to perennial surface waters, but nonetheless serve as sites of groundwater recharge and discharge, making them critical to the overall water budget at regional scales. Thus, legal protections for ephemeral waters will vary from project to project, based on site-specific surface hydrology that may not reflect their landscape-level function.

Given their importance and susceptibility to impacts, it is critical to develop criteria to evaluate ephemeral waters based on their habitat quality and ecological functions (Brady and Vyverberg 2014). The criteria could be used to avoid those aquatic features with higher ecological value and to inform adaptive management actions by providing quantitative indices that are indicative of negative impacts from solar energy development. In addition, one limitation of existing state and federal permitting is that the required avoidance and mitigation measures are decided on a case-

by-case basis, which makes it difficult for developers to make siting decisions and anticipate regulatory costs. Developing criteria for predictably and consistently determining which ephemeral surface waters to avoid would therefore be beneficial to all stakeholders (Brady and Vyverberg 2014).

Habitat assessments are commonly used to prioritize the conservation of aquatic systems (Barbour et al. 1999; Miller et al. 1988). Typically, these assessments use sitespecific geomorphology, surrounding land cover, water quality, and biological community structure to rate the functional value of the stream or water body (Kerans and Karr 1994). However, the temporary flows and harsh conditions in ephemeral streams would generally not permit the use of most commonly used indicator species or physical and chemical indicators of habitat quality. Consequently, a unique set of valuation criteria is needed to assess dryland aquatic habitats.

Multiple physical and biological functions should be considered in evaluating intermittent ephemeral waters. The hydrologic characteristics and functions of the stream or water body should be a primary component of the evaluation. Caruso (2011) proposed criteria for establishing a significant nexus with jurisdictional waters based on the hydrologic role of the ephemeral waters in supporting larger stream networks that included considerations of stream order, flow duration, hydrologic connectivity to perennial streams, and annual discharge. Other potential physical indicators of habitat quality include streams with soils or geomorphology appropriate for the many burrowing species of desert reptiles, birds, and mammals to create areas for nesting or shelter (Levick et al. 2008). Potential biological indicators include aquatic invertebrate abundance and species composition, which are sensitive to the frequency and duration of flow (Sponseller et al. 2010), and the connectivity of these populations to communities in downstream intermittent and perennial waters (Graham 2002). The primary biological indicator of ecological value in desert environments is likely to be riparian habitat condition, which provides information on flow regime (Stromberg et al. 2006), nutrient and organic matter exports (McClain et al. 2003), and the value of the site to terrestrial wildlife (Levick et al. 2008). Potential riparian habitat quality indicators include plant density, patch size and connectivity, proximity to land disturbance, fragmentation, and the proportion of invasive species.

Unfortunately, evaluating many of these parameters is not possible at present and will require significant regional data collection. For example, ephemeral stream networks are not adequately mapped in commonly used GIS databases such as the National Hydrography Dataset (Caruso and Haynes 2011). Therefore, additional remote sensing with field validation will be essential in evaluating the

hydrologic functions and connectivity of ephemeral streams. There is also little research on invertebrate communities in ephemeral waters, making it difficult to assess their utility as an indicator of habitat quality. Similarly, the ability to assess riparian habitat quality is limited by a lack of high-resolution vegetation mapping.

## Conclusion

Without proper management and planning, commercialscale solar energy facilities could contribute to existing water resource stressors in the Southwestern United States. To avoid this outcome, solar facility development should avoid high-value aquatic habitat and implement construction and operational management practices that minimize impacts on aquatic habitat and biota. In achieving this objective, basic research conducted within an adaptive monitoring and management framework is needed to characterize the realized impacts of these projects and assess the effectiveness of mitigation policies. Currently, the ecological and hydrologic inventory of intermittent and ephemeral surface waters is limited in this region of the United States. Therefore, new research and data collection will be required to determine areas of high ecological value or vulnerability to impacts, to which avoidance and/or monitoring resources should be directed.
